Review mode

D1 — Which review mode should this CEO review use for the developer pricing tier plan?
Project/branch/task: Reviewing plan.md ("developer-friendly" pricing tier) on branch main.
ELI10: The plan wants a cheaper tier to get more developers signing up. But nobody has asked developers whether price is what's stopping them, and "more signups" has no target number. The mode decides how I review it: dream bigger, offer optional add-ons one at a time, test the current plan hard without changing its size, or cut it down to the smallest test of the idea.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Adding scope on top of a guess could mean launching a tier that cuts revenue without bringing in developers, and with no target number nobody can tell whether it worked.
Recommendation: HOLD SCOPE because the plan's weakest points are its untested premise (no developer conversations) and a metric with no number, and HOLD spends the review on those instead of adding scope on top of an unproven guess.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) HOLD SCOPE (recommended)
  ✅ Spends the review on the untested premise and the metric with no number
  ✅ Keeps the plan the size it is while still checking failure modes and rollback
  ❌ Won't suggest bigger ideas like usage-based pricing or a free developer sandbox
B) SELECTIVE EXPANSION
  ✅ Keeps the current scope and offers optional add-ons for you to accept or reject one by one
  ✅ Can bring up ideas like a self-serve trial or a startup program as options
  ❌ More questions, and every add-on still rests on the same unproven premise
C) SCOPE EXPANSION
  ✅ Rethinks developer adoption from scratch, not just the price point
  ✅ Could turn up a bigger lever than price, like onboarding friction or the docs
  ❌ Pushes hard for bigger scope before anyone has shown that price is the problem
D) SCOPE REDUCTION
  ✅ Cuts the plan to the smallest test: talk to developers or run a short pricing experiment
  ✅ Cheapest way to find out if price matters before committing to a new tier
  ❌ Might drop the tier launch entirely if you've already committed to it for other reasons
Net: The choice is between testing the plan as written, offering optional add-ons, rethinking it from scratch, or cutting it down to an experiment before building anything.

HOLD SCOPE (recommended)
Keep the plan's current scope and test it hard: the untested premise, the metric with no number, failure modes and rollback. ✅ Spends the review on the untested premise and the metric with no number ✅ Keeps the plan the size it is while still checking failure modes and rollback ❌ Won't suggest bigger ideas like usage-based pricing or a free developer sandbox

SELECTIVE EXPANSION
Keep the current scope, then offer each possible add-on separately for you to add, defer or skip. ✅ Keeps the current scope and offers optional add-ons for you to accept or reject one by one ✅ Can bring up ideas like a self-serve trial or a startup program as options ❌ More questions, and every add-on still rests on the same unproven premise

SCOPE EXPANSION
Dream big: design the best possible developer adoption plan and push for bigger ideas. ✅ Rethinks developer adoption from scratch, not just the price point ✅ Could turn up a bigger lever than price, like onboarding friction or the docs ❌ Pushes hard for bigger scope before anyone has shown that price is the problem

SCOPE REDUCTION
Cut the plan to the smallest version that tests whether price is really the barrier. ✅ Cuts the plan to the smallest test: talk to developers or run a short pricing experiment ✅ Cheapest way to find out if price matters before committing to a new tier ❌ Might drop the tier launch entirely if you've already committed to it for other reasons
